title: Raytheon Books $6.3B SM-3 Deal While Its Coyote Counter-Drone Family Goes Export
subhead: Raytheon secures a five-year SM-3 IB interceptor contract worth up to $6.3 billion and lands the first international sales of its Coyote effectors and KuRFS sensor with Qatar and Jordan, cementing the shift toward mass-producible missile defense and counter-drone inventories.

sections.heading: Raytheon Wins $6.3 Billion SM-3 IB Interceptor Contract
sections.body:
The US Department of Defense has awarded Raytheon a five-year contract valued at up to $6.3 billion to produce and sustain Standard Missile-3 Block IB (SM-3 IB) interceptors, according to The Defense Post. The contract includes two additional option years and flows out of five landmark agreements Raytheon signed with the Department of Defense in February 2026 to accelerate production and replenish missile defense inventories.

The award follows a $24.4 billion five-year Raytheon contract to build Standard Missile-6 (SM-6) interceptors for the US Navy, reported earlier this month. While both are ship-launched, the SM-3 is optimized to intercept ballistic missiles in midcourse flight, whereas the SM-6 covers a broader air and missile defense envelope. Raytheon President Phil Jasper framed the award as part of the company's push to increase output of critical munitions.
sections.whyItMatters: The SM-3 and SM-6 awards together commit roughly $30 billion to a single supplier for ship-launched interceptors. Washington is locking in multi-year production ahead of demand rather than buying in annual increments — a structural change in how the US rebuilds missile defense stockpiles after the Iran-Gulf confrontation drained inventories.

sections.heading: Coyote and KuRFS Enter the Export Market With Qatar and Jordan
sections.body:
Raytheon has won $729 million in contracts to supply counter-drone equipment to the US Army, Qatar and Jordan, per defence-industry.eu. The awards include the first international sales of its Coyote effectors and Ku-band Radio Frequency Sensor (KuRFS), both components of the Army's LIDS (Low, slow, small, unmanned aircraft Integrated Defeat System).

KuRFS provides 360-degree threat detection, while Coyote kinetic and non-kinetic effectors engage individual drones and swarms across fixed-site and mobile configurations. Raytheon says Coyote has achieved hundreds of combat intercepts. The company did not disclose quantities ordered, delivery schedules, or how the $729 million splits among the three customers. Regional urgency stems partly from Iranian drone attacks that damaged sites in US-allied Gulf countries, which highlighted shortfalls in available interceptor stocks.
sections.whyItMatters: This is counter-drone hardware moving from a US-only capability to an export product. Gulf states that absorbed Iranian drone strikes are now buying the same layered defense the US Army uses — a sign that drone defense is becoming a standard line item in Middle East procurement, not an emergency add-on.

sections.heading: Raytheon Tests Faster Coyote Variant as Counter-Drone Demand Surges
sections.body:
Raytheon has completed three tests of its Coyote Block 2C+RM upgrades, taking the variant from concept to testing in 15 months on company funding, according to defence-industry.eu. The upgrade adds propulsion improvements for faster launch and flight, a new seeker, and a new kinetic warhead. The first test series confirmed integration with the existing counter-drone architecture and included the first launches of a Coyote effector fitted with a tactical rocket motor meant to shorten engagement times and permit faster successive shots.

A parallel variant, Block 3NK, uses a non-kinetic payload to defeat drone swarms while reducing collateral damage; it can loiter, return after an engagement, and be redeployed. Raytheon said Block 3NK defeated multiple swarms during a US Army demonstration earlier this year. Tom Laliberty, president of Land & Air Defense Systems at Raytheon, said a shared 'common backbone' lets the company scale the Coyote family across counter-drone missions. Raytheon did not disclose a Block 2C+RM fielding date.
sections.whyItMatters: Self-funded, 15-month development cycles signal that drone-defense upgrades are now paced by commercial urgency rather than the traditional acquisition timetable. The kinetic-plus-recoverable split also reflects a maturing doctrine: cheap fast interceptors for single drones, reusable non-kinetic effectors for swarms.

sections.heading: NATO Opens Steadfast Noon Nuclear Drill With 17 Nations
sections.body:
NATO began its annual nuclear deterrence exercise, Steadfast Noon, on October 13 with personnel from 17 Alliance countries, per DPA via glavnoe.in.ua. The drills run until the end of next week and focus on defending Alliance territory using nuclear forces. Germany deployed three Tornado fighter-bombers from Tactical Air Wing 33 to Aviano Air Base in northern Italy, along with several dozen German service members.

The Tornados are normally stationed at Büchel Air Base in Rhineland-Palatinate, where US nuclear weapons are stored under unofficial but widely reported NATO nuclear-sharing arrangements. Separately, NATO's top military commander, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, warned Russia that the alliance would 'block, blunt and break' enemy forces if attacked, as reported by the New York Post.
sections.whyItMatters: The exercise keeps nuclear-sharing mechanics — German aircraft, US warheads, Italian basing — visible at a moment of elevated Russia-NATO tension. The combination of a public nuclear drill and blunt deterrence messaging is calibrated signaling rather than a posture change, but it reinforces that NATO's nuclear-sharing infrastructure remains central to its deterrent.

sections.heading: India's Akash SAM Confirmed as Export to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan
sections.body:
Indian Defense Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed that Tajikistan and Turkmenistan are new customers for India's indigenous Akash medium-range mobile surface-to-air missile system, in comments to ANI reported by The Diplomat. Singh said Armenia was the first customer and has taken multiple batteries, with Tajikistan and Turkmenistan following.

Neither Central Asian country has publicly commented, though a July report in BW Businessworld had already listed them as Akash export destinations citing official data. Central Asia's militaries are diversifying suppliers: Turkmenistan displayed a newly acquired Chinese FK-2000 air-defense system at its September 27 Independence Day parade, alongside a Brazilian A-29 Super Tucano and Italian Leonardo M-346 jets, while Tajikistan has shown China's HQ-17AE system and Chinese armored vehicles. India also reviewed its defense cooperation program with Cyprus, discussing 2027 priorities.
sections.whyItMatters: India is proving it can sell air-defense systems into Central Asia, a region long dominated by Russian equipment. The mix of Indian, Chinese, Brazilian, and Italian hardware on display shows supplier competition is now the norm — a quiet erosion of Russia's traditional role as the region's arms source.

sections.heading: US Navy Scopes Shipyards for Next-Generation SSN(X) Submarine
sections.body:
The US Navy is assessing domestic shipyard capacity to support construction of its next-generation SSN(X) nuclear-powered attack submarine, according to Naval Today. The move signals the service is moving toward industrial-base planning for the follow-on to the Virginia-class, which remains constrained by shipyard throughput.

Separately, President Trump said at a Youngstown rally that Cleveland has been selected as the site of a new submarine repair center, though details remain scarce, per Ideastream Public Media.
sections.whyItMatters: Both items point at the same bottleneck: US submarine industrial capacity, not design. The Navy is scoping yards for a future class while the President touts a repair hub — a recognition that sustaining and expanding the undersea fleet depends as much on infrastructure and workforce as on new platforms.

sections.heading: Pentagon Pushes Cheaper Hypersonics as Costs Draw Scrutiny
sections.body:
The Pentagon is pressing to expand hypersonic production while defense startups race to cut unit costs, per Fox News. GAO estimates put the Army's long-range hypersonic weapon, Dark Eagle, at more than $40 million per missile, while the Navy's effort to arm Zumwalt destroyers with hypersonics is estimated at $70 million per missile including development — and is reportedly two years behind schedule.

For comparison, a Tomahawk costs about $2.6 million, a Patriot roughly $4 million, and a Precision Strike Missile about $1.6 million. CSIS senior advisor Mark Cancian told Fox News the US needs 'all three tiers of missiles — the cheap ones, the ones that are now the high-end like Patriot and then maybe some hypersonics,' while UC Berkeley's Cameron Tracy noted hypersonics are now seen as the novel system and ballistic missiles as the archaic one.
sections.whyItMatters: Hypersonics remain a low-volume, high-cost segment. The cost gap — roughly 25 to 27 conventional missiles per hypersonic round — is the real constraint on fielding them at scale, which is why startup-led cost reduction, not just performance, is now the Pentagon's stated priority.

bottomLine: Raytheon had the day: a $6.3 billion SM-3 IB contract plus the first export sales of its Coyote and KuRFS counter-drone gear to Qatar and Jordan show how the US and its Gulf partners are industrializing missile and drone defense into multi-year, multi-billion production lines. Around that, NATO's Steadfast Noon drill kept nuclear sharing visible, India confirmed Central Asian buyers for its Akash air-defense system, and the Navy moved toward scoping yards for the next attack submarine. The through-line is production capacity — interceptors, counter-drone effectors, submarines, and hypersonics all hinge less on technology than on whether industry can build them at volume and at viable cost.
sources: The Defense Post, defence-industry.eu, DPA via glavnoe.in.ua, New York Post, The Diplomat, ANI, BW Businessworld, RFE/RL, Naval Today, Ideastream Public Media, Fox News, US GAO, CSIS
